title: Three Red Notes Beyond the Factory Gate
teaser: The new refrigerator could accept only three more environmental improvements before the design was locked at month-end. Zhou He first placed all three red notes inside her own factory, then discovered that the three largest internal numbers were not necessarily the three impacts most worth addressing first.
paragraphs: On Monday morning, Zhou He was preparing the final launch review for a compact refrigerator. Once the month ended, the mold design and supplier contracts would be locked, and headquarters would fund only three environmental improvements. The production team gave her a factory layout marked with annual figures for assembly electricity, packaging offcuts, and testing-line losses. Each figure came with a clear owner and an estimated improvement cost. For years, the company had chosen projects from this map: things it could measure itself, control itself, and show in next month’s report. Zhou He placed three red notes beside the largest numbers and planned to sign off on Friday.

On Tuesday, the final batch of pre-launch trial photos arrived. One refrigerator had been pushed into a cabinet recess in a student apartment, leaving only two centimeters between its back panel and the wall. The manual said only to “maintain adequate clearance,” and the resident had not modified the product. Test staff recreated the setup. The same unit ran noticeably longer each day with the two-centimeter gap, then returned toward its previous runtime when it was pulled forward. R&D estimated that if the rear airflow design remained unchanged, the extra electricity use in such installations would continue for years of product use. Changing the airflow design would consume one of the three improvement budgets. Zhou He peeled the red note from “testing-line loss” and placed it temporarily at the edge of the photograph.

That evening, procurement brought in a price-lock document for the new compressor assembly. The assembly was lighter and cheaper, but two critical metals could currently be traced only as far as the tier-one suppliers. If the team demanded mine-level traceability for every material before month-end, the contract would not be signed in time. If it asked nothing, it would not know where the risk was concentrated. Zhou He did not order unlimited tracing. She asked procurement to add only three things: supply concentration for the two metals, whatever sourcing records the tier-one suppliers already held, and the information clauses that could realistically be added in the next contract round. The second red note left “packaging offcuts” and landed beside the names of those two metals.

On Wednesday, the recycling team dismantled an older model. One connector held them up for more than ten minutes; when it could not be released efficiently, recyclers usually crushed the entire module instead. Zhou He spread a long sheet of paper beside the factory map and drew the product path from materials and components through assembly, use, repair, and end of life. She then reconsidered every candidate project using the same questions: the size and duration of the impact, the information available, and the degree of influence the company could realistically exercise. Packaging offcuts were large in volume, but a stable recycling route already existed. The internal testing line was directly controllable, but the improvement per unit was limited. The two-centimeter installation effect could persist for years; supply of the two metals was highly concentrated; and the connector repeatedly affected disassembly. The third red note also crossed the factory-gate line drawn through the middle of the sheet.

At Friday’s meeting, the production manager still argued for keeping the testing-line project. Its result was certain, ownership was clear, and it would help the plant meet its annual energy target. Zhou He did not dismiss the project. Under the unchanged limit of three budgets, however, she left the red notes on the rear airflow design, the information requirements for the two critical metals, and the connector redesign. The costs now fell directly on her own company: the mold needed one more revision, procurement took on two extra weeks of negotiation work, and the plant lost one contribution to its annual energy target. Nor did the team suddenly gain control over every user and upstream company. It used only the levers it actually had—product design, contracts, and focused information requests—at the points judged most important.

Three months after launch, unit energy use inside the factory was almost unchanged from the old model, so the plant’s monthly report did not look much better. Elsewhere, the recreated tight-space test showed lower runtime; two tier-one suppliers provided additional information on the critical metals, and one accepted stricter sourcing clauses for the next contract round; during recycling trials, the new connector reduced removal time from more than ten minutes to only a few. Zhou He placed the original factory map underneath the long product-path sheet. Three old adhesive marks were still visible inside the factory. On the right side of the long sheet, a small red box labeled “2 cm” sat just beyond the factory-gate line.
concept: A sustainability value-chain perspective requires companies to identify significant impacts, risks, and opportunities not only in their own operations but also in upstream supply relationships and in downstream stages such as use, repair, recycling, and disposal. The legal-entity boundary and the boundary of direct control are not the same as the boundary of impact. Assessment therefore cannot select projects only from activities that are easiest for the company itself to measure and control. It must identify significant points along the value chain and business relationships, then set priorities in light of information availability and the company’s actual ability to exert influence.
explanation: The normal baseline is to choose improvements only inside the company’s own factory because the data is complete, ownership is clear, and results are easy to show in monthly reporting. The behavioral shift is not that “internal projects do not matter.” It is that Zhou He extends the same materiality judgment along the product path to upstream materials, the use phase, and end of life. The three-budget limit never changes, and the team never gains unlimited data, so it acts only on three areas judged more significant, using feasible levers such as design, contracts, and focused information requirements. In the end, internal metrics barely improve while impacts at other points in the value chain do.
mapping: All three red notes begin beside the factory’s largest numbers → The normal baseline treats direct operations as the main assessment boundary.
A two-centimeter gap increases runtime during the use phase → A significant impact can arise downstream even when the company cannot control every user.

The team traces only two critical metals and adds future contract requirements → Upstream assessment is focused according to significance and available information rather than requiring unlimited tracing through every tier.

The factory’s monthly report barely changes while use-phase, sourcing-information, and disassembly outcomes improve → Internal indicators alone can miss more significant results elsewhere in the value chain.
boundary: Value-chain assessment does not require a company to assume unlimited responsibility for every supplier, customer, or end user, nor does it require complete data on every stage before a decision can be made. Companies still need to set priorities according to significance of impact, business relationships, information availability, and their ability to exert influence. The story compresses three value-chain stages into one product and does not imply that they are always more important than factory improvements. Real priorities must be determined from the specific evidence.
reflection: If the three red notes were never allowed to cross the factory-gate line, which long-term impacts would remain outside the picture simply because “we do not directly control them”?
